Conversation field guide · 2–11 July 2026

Two useful verb patterns

Across these 10 sessions, two correction patterns recur in at least three distinct sessions. Both concern the form that follows an expression. Some other suggested changes are optional—or would change a correct original.

Choose a focus. Each has one optional application; you can switch or stop at any time.

Focus 1 · Verb structure

Suggest an action, not “someone to…”

Original · from your records

She suggested me to take a break.

Revision

She suggested that I take a break.

Reusable rule suggest + that + person + verb

For a recommendation, suggest does not normally take someone + to + verb. Use a that-clause to say who should act. Here, that I take makes it clear that I am the person taking the break.

“She suggested taking a break” also works when the person doing it is clear from context. Keep suggested: the problem is the structure after it, not its past tense.

Optional application · new teaching example

Pass on a recommendation

Your colleague thinks you should contact the hotel. Choose the sentence that fits.

“My colleague suggested…”

Source trail & a useful alternative

Where this appears

The same original/revision pair shown above is recorded in four distinct sessions. This is recurrence of one sentence, not four different sentence examples.

Sources: N01-U03 · N04-U03 · N07-U03 · N10-U03

Another valid form

“She suggested that I should take a break” is also possible. The key distinction remains: use a clause after suggest, not me to take.

New teaching alternative based on the source sentence.

Focus 2 · After a preposition

After “interested in,” use an -ing form

Original · from your records

I am interested in learn more about plants.

Revision

I am interested in learning more about plants.

Reusable rule interested in + verb-ing

When a verb follows the preposition in, use its -ing form. Here, learning names the activity you are interested in; it does not mean the activity is happening right now.

Keep “I am interested in” and the rest of the sentence. A noun can follow in too: “I am interested in plants.” (New teaching example.)

Optional application · new teaching example

Talk about a possible hobby

You want to try photography. Choose the form that fits after in.

“I’m interested in…”

Source trail & a correct form to keep

Where this appears

The same original/revision pair shown above is recorded in three distinct sessions. The evidence supports this specific expression; it does not establish a problem with every preposition.

Sources: N02-U03 · N05-U03 · N08-U03

Keep “looking forward to seeing”

Your recorded sentence “I am looking forward to seeing you” is correct. In look forward to, to is a preposition, so seeing is the right form. The proposed change to see should not be used.

Sources: N04-U01 · N10-U01

Why only these two focuses?

Recurrence means separate sessions

The past-tense corrections go → went, buy → bought, and see → saw are valid for those completed past events. But all three come from one session, so they are not treated as a recurring pattern here.

Sources: N06-U03 · N06-U04 · N06-U05

A suggestion is not always a correction

“I think the plan is pretty good” is grammatical casual English. “Because I was tired” is a natural answer to “Why did you stop?” Neither needs the proposed expansion or formal wording.

Sources: N01-U01 · N07-U01; N02-U01 · N08-U01

“I have a little time this evening” correctly means some time is available. Removing a would change that meaning to almost none.

Sources: N03-U01 · N09-U01
